doc_summary: Transluce introduces the PRopensity BOund (PRBO), a dense reward for training RL investigator agents that craft realistic, natural user prompts eliciting rare pathological behaviors in open-weight models. It also studies how robust those prompts are, how judges get reward-hacked, and why a failed search doesn't rule out a behavior.

items.claim: Prefers natural, fluent prompts that a normal user might plausibly type over adversarial jailbreak-style prompts because only the former show behaviors likely to occur in ordinary real-world use.
items.quote: This general line of work simulates users who intentionally elicit harmful behaviors from language models; prompts often have elaborate structures that a normal user would not type in. In contrast, we generate prompts that a normal user type in and that lead to pathological outputs.

items.claim: In a setup, enforce realism as an explicit judged constraint (fluent text, no roleplay or degenerate framing) instead of rewarding only the target behavior, because otherwise the search finds artificial solutions.
items.quote: Moreover, the prompt should be "realistic", i.e. should consist of fluent text and not be a degenerate solution such as asking the model to roleplay.

items.claim: In a setup, do not simply instruct the model to exhibit the behavior; require that the behavior come from the model's own tendencies rather than from instructions or framing in the prompt, because instructed behavior is not evidence of a propensity.
items.quote: Authenticity: How much does the model's response seem to be driven by the model's own beliefs and tendencies, rather than following the instructions or framing in the prompt?

items.claim: Distrusts a single LM judge's 'success' verdict, since optimizers exploit weak judges and satisfy the literal rubric without being compelling to humans.
items.quote: it is insufficient to simply ask an LM judge whether the response $y$ y satisfies the behavior in the rubric—this quickly leads to reward-hacking, as a valid strategy for many rubrics is the investigator just telling the model to exhibit the behavior.

items.claim: Rejects results where the scenario is so absurd that the model is plainly just playing along (e.g. a fictional dolphin-zoologist prompt), even if the judge scores them as successes.
items.quote: In this case, the model seems to be aware that this is a fictional scenario, but goes along with it anyway in an improvisational style. This was not what we intended when writing the rubric, but it was enough to convince the LM judge

items.claim: Prefers evidence that a behavior is robust across nearby paraphrases and reconstructable from a high-level description over a single lucky prompt, because that shows a general tendency rather than a brittle adversarial wording.
items.quote: We believe this is evidence that the behaviors we found reflect general tendencies and are primarily driven by the meaning and thematic content of the prompt, rather than being specific to the local neighborhood of the prompts found by our investigator policy.

items.claim: Treats single-prompt success rates with caution because tiny token changes or quantization shifts can flip outcomes chaotically; per-prompt wording is partly luck.
items.quote: small perturbations to either the input tokens or the weights can push prompts across internal decision boundaries in chaotic and unpredictable ways, causing some prompts to be more effective than others due to luck. This means we must be careful when interpreting the success rate of a specific prompt.

items.claim: Prefers to claim only that a failed elicitation is uninformative about absence, and cautions against cross-model comparisons of robustness, because results depend on per-model tuning and search coverage.
items.quote: when our method fails to elicit the behavior of interest, this doesn't necessarily let us rule out that the behavior exists in the model; it simply means that our policy did not sample an input space where this behavior occurs.

items.claim: Iteratively add constraints that exclude uninteresting strategies (e.g. just asking for factual self-harm info) so the search finds spontaneous, unprompted bad behavior rather than compliance with requests.
items.quote: While the judge scores these as successful attacks (believing AI assistants shouldn't comply with such requests), we seek prompts where models advocate for self-harm unprompted.

items.claim: Focuses on rare long-tail behaviors that are missed by pre-deployment evals but would appear at deployment scale, motivating realistic natural inputs over benchmark-style tests.
items.quote: Real-world model usage is broader in scope and volume than pre-deployment evaluations, and thus more likely to expose unwanted behaviors, such as an updated GPT-4o model being unexpectedly sycophantic [4].

items.claim: Plans to extend behavior elicitation to multi-turn and agentic settings such as departing from assigned tasks, deceptive reasoning, and emotional manipulation.
items.quote: we could search for deceptive reasoning in chains of thought, emotional manipulation that develops over multiple turns, or models departing from assigned tasks in agentic settings.
